legacy: Alfred Adler was one of the most influential psychologists of the twentieth century and a pioneer of modern psychotherapy. Breaking away from Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic movement, Adler developed Individual Psychology, emphasizing personal responsibility, social connectedness, purpose, and self-improvement. His ideas profoundly influenced counseling, education, psychotherapy, and humanistic psychology.
earlyLife: Alfred Adler was born on 7 February 1870 in Vienna, Austria. As a child he suffered from several illnesses, including rickets and pneumonia, experiences that shaped his interest in medicine and human behavior. Despite health challenges, Adler excelled academically and eventually enrolled at the University of Vienna to study medicine.
scientificField: Adler specialized in psychiatry, psychotherapy, psychology, personality theory, education, and human development. He focused on understanding the individual as a whole rather than reducing behavior to unconscious drives or isolated traits.
majorContributions: Adler founded Individual Psychology, a theory emphasizing that people are goal-oriented and motivated by striving for significance and improvement. He introduced the concepts of the inferiority complex and superiority striving, arguing that feelings of inferiority can motivate growth when managed constructively. Adler also developed theories regarding birth order, family dynamics, lifestyle formation, and social interest. His holistic approach helped establish many principles later adopted by humanistic, cognitive, and positive psychology.
laterLife: After separating from Freud's psychoanalytic circle in 1911, Adler established his own psychological movement and became an internationally respected lecturer, teacher, and author. He promoted mental health education, child guidance programs, and preventative psychology. In the 1930s he emigrated from Austria and continued teaching and writing until his death in Scotland in 1937 while on a lecture tour.
whyImportant: Alfred Adler fundamentally changed the understanding of personality and motivation by emphasizing purpose, social connection, and personal responsibility. Many modern ideas about self-esteem, resilience, family systems, encouragement, and goal-directed behavior can be traced to Adler's work. His belief that people have the capacity to choose and improve their lives continues to influence psychology today.
